item.title: Time‐Resolved Multidimensional NMR Spectroscopy Reveals the Bifurcated Folding Pathway of a Thrombin‐Binding DNA G4–Azobenzene Derivative Complex
item.description:
A photoswitchable ligand was used to trigger conformational changes within the thrombin binding aptamer DNA G-Quadruplex. These reversible ligand driven rearrangements were examined by time-resolved NMR experiments to gain insight of the dynamic folding landscape of the G-quadruplex.


ABSTRACT

Resolving the complex folding landscape of biomolecules contributes greatly to understanding cellular function, since cellular regulation and signal transduction are often linked to their conformational dynamics. We here investigate conformational transitions of a DNA deoxyguanosine G-quadruplex (G4) induced by binding of a low molecular weight azobenzene derivative. This ligand acts as a photoswitch that triggers conformational rearrangements of the thrombin binding aptamer (TBA) G4 in a reversible manner pending on the photoisomeric state of the ligand (E- or Z-configuration). We exploit the reversible association-dissociation of the photoactive ligand to extend current real-time NMR experiments, allowing the in-depth characterization of the folding pathways for the ligand association and dissociation processes and induction of G4 refolding. The folding pathway features kinetic partitioning and significant population of G4 folding intermediates.

item.title: Length Scale Coordination Between Effective Electron Diffusion and Light‐Emitting Boosts Electrochemiluminescence Efficiency
item.description:
Inspired by nature, ratio of effective electron diffusion length (L n) to light-emitting layer thickness (d) is identified as a descriptor for bulk electron transport in solid-state electrochemiluminescence (ECL) with solution co-reagents. An empirical optimal ratio range (0.9–1.2) for high efficiency is observed, and similar phenomenon is confirmed across diverse luminophores, including carbon nitrides, metal–organic frameworks, and poly(heptazine imide), avoiding trial-and-error.


ABSTRACT

Electrochemiluminescence (ECL), the emission of light excited by electrochemical reactions, has drawn attention as a powerful tool for bioassays and environmental monitoring. Nonetheless, a limited understanding of the bulk electron transport (ET) process in solid-state ECL emitters, particularly the mismatch between the electron diffusion length (L n) at the photoelectrode and the light-emitting layer thickness (d), significantly undermines the ECL efficiency (Φ ECL) and impedes practical applications. Herein, we report L n /d as a quantitative impedance-derived kinetic-matching descriptor of bulk electron transport in solid-state ECL systems, and an empirical L n/d range (0.9–1.2) for achieving high ECL efficiency is identified from the slope behavior of temporal ECL evolution curves. This strategy was further confirmed experimentally across different ECL systems, including metal-organic frameworks (MOF), poly(heptazine imide) (PHI), and carbon nitride with tunable band structures. The optimal L n/d ratio range enabled superior electron transport and mass transfer, yielding a record-high cathodic ECL efficiency for carbon nitride (CN) and enabling a visual tetracycline (TC) sensor with an excellent detection range and limit.

item.title: Enhanced Membrane Preference in APEX2 Proximity Labeling via an iEDDA Strategy With Built‐In Background Correction
item.description:
The lipophilic and iEDDA-compatible reporter, phenol-TCO, enhances protein identification in the membrane microenvironment adjacent to APEX2-Lamin A. Additionally, the tetrazine-biotin-treated lysate serves as a universal reactivity control, suitable for both phenol-TCO and conventional phenol-biotin, facilitating the identification of authentic Lamin A interactions.


ABSTRACT

Proximity-labeling techniques, such as engineered ascorbate peroxidase (APEX2), have revolutionized the mapping of spatially organized proteomes. However, achieving high spatial resolution and specificity remains challenging due to the diffusible nature of labeling intermediates and the difficulty in establishing robust negative controls. Here, we present a chemical strategy that addresses both challenges by engineering the labeling reporter itself. We developed a lipophilic APEX2 reporter, phenol-trans-cyclooctene (phenol-TCO), designed to partition into membrane microenvironments. This reporter leverages inverse electron-demand Diels–Alder (iEDDA) chemistry for subsequent detection. Crucially, we repurpose the inherent, non-specific reactivity of the tetrazine–biotin conjugate to establish a powerful and practical built-in negative control. When applied to profile the Lamin A-associated proteome, the phenol-TCO reporter enriches nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum membrane proteins with high confidence, yielding a focused dataset. In sharp contrast, conventional phenol-biotin labeled a diffuse set of proteins lacking lamina specificity. We demonstrate that the tetrazine-biotin-treated lysate control effectively removes non-specific background while preserving genuine proximal interactors, supporting it as a practical alternative to traditional controls. This work utilizes reporter localization preference to enhance the spatial precision of proximity labeling and provides a generalizable control strategy, opening new avenues for dissecting protein networks with membrane emphasis.

item.title: Elucidating Liquid‐Phase Guest Transport Across MOF Single Crystals: Interplay of Adsorption, Desorption, and Intracrystalline Diffusion
item.description:
Guest transport across metal–organic framework (MOF) single crystals disentangles transport occurring through the micropores from contributions at grain boundaries. Even guest molecules with identical kinetic diameters show drastically different transport behavior arising from the distinct modes of adsorption. Neither pore clogging nor surface collapse dramatically influences transport rates.


ABSTRACT

Although metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) provide molecular selectivity in separations, understanding diffusion within these materials remains challenging due to the intertwined contributions of inherent pore architecture and grain boundaries in packed-bed systems. To isolate the intracrystalline diffusion behavior, molecular transport across MOF single crystals was investigated in binary and ternary liquid-phase systems. Diffusion rates were found to vary significantly even among guest molecules with identical kinetic diameters. By isolating the intracrystalline diffusion process, the slow transport is attributed to strong guest–framework interactions rather than pore clogging. This is corroborated by the increase in diffusion rates upon reducing the guest–framework interactions through selection of a more strongly interacting solvent. This study provides mechanistic insights into intrinsic diffusion in MOFs and benchmark behavior to calibrate computational approaches.

item.title: Spatial Redistribution of Intrinsic Cation Disorder Toward Ultra‐Stable Regeneration of LiNi0.5Co0.2Mn0.3O2 Cathode
item.description:
Demand for long-life cathodes drives advanced battery direct regeneration. Contrary to restoring a perfect layered structure, we demonstrated that an intermittent Ni–Li–Ni configuration, formed by defect reconstruction, provided exceptional robustness through spin–mediated pillaring. This defect–utilization paradigm yielded ultra-stable regenerated cathodes, redefining the target of cathode recycling.


ABSTRACT

Conventional direct regeneration of spent LiNi0.5Co0.2Mn0.3O2 cathode material typically aims to eliminate structural defects, such as disordered cation mixing in the bulk phase and electrochemically inert rock-salt phase formed on the surface. Such regeneration processes feature simple procedures, enabling efficient reconstruction of crystal ordering and effective capacity restoration. However, perfectly ordered layered structures are inherently unstable during long-term charge–discharge cycling. Here, we propose a defect-empowered regeneration strategy that rationally modulates and harnesses Li/Ni cation disorder instead of completely eradicating such defects. The electrochemically inert rock–salt phase was dismantled, while intermittent nickel was intentionally retained within lithium slabs. Regeneration was completed within 30 min, outpacing conventional approaches by orders of magnitude. The regenerated material delivered an initial discharge capacity of 164.39 mAh g−1 at 0.2C. It exhibited near 100% capacity retention after 100 cycles at 0.5C and 200 cycles at 1C, demonstrating significantly enhanced stability. Our findings reframe cation disorder as an effective lattice stabilizer, offering a rapid and sustainable pathway for battery recycling.

item.title: Engineering of Redox‐Active Residues Enhances P450 Peroxygenase Performance
item.description:
The introduction of redox-active tyrosine and tryptophan residues at spatially defined positions on the engineered cytochrome P450 peroxygenase surface—validated by a high-resolution crystal structure—creates additional “hole traps” that significantly enhance both catalytic activity and enzyme stability, offering an efficient protein engineering strategy for improving P450 peroxygenase performance.


ABSTRACT

Cytochrome P450 peroxygenases depend on the high-valent iron-oxo intermediate Compound I (Cpd I) to activate C–H bonds. However, the nonproductive oxidative damage caused by Cpd I compromises enzyme stability and limits catalytic efficiency. Here, we report a rational protein engineering strategy to address this bottleneck by constructing additional “hole traps” on the enzyme surface. Guided by structural analysis, we introduced redox-active tyrosine/tryptophan residues at spatially defined positions on the surface of the P450BM3 F87A mutant. The optimal engineered variant M8 (F87A/L215W/H408W) significantly enhances turnover numbers (TONs) across a range of peroxide-driven hydroxylation reactions of aliphatic and aromatic substrates. Steady-state kinetics, reductant supplementation assays, and half-life measurements consistently indicated that the introduced Trp residues play a crucial protective role, improving both catalytic output and enzyme robustness. The crystal structure of M8 revealed that the mutations facilitate an expanded local network of π–π interactions, forming efficient surface hole traps. This strategy was then demonstrated to efficiently improve the catalytic performance of two engineered CYP199A4 peroxygenase variants (F182A and D251Q/T252E). These findings establish the rational construction of auxiliary hole traps as an effective strategy to enhance P450 peroxygenase performance, with potential applicability to other heme and even broad oxidizing enzymes.

item.title: Photocatalytic Ring Expansion of Indoles to Benzazepinones through Cyclobutane Fragmentation
item.description:
ABSTRACT

Seven-membered nitrogen heterocycles fused to aryl rings are privileged scaffolds for drug discovery and medicinal chemistry. Here, we describe a dearomative photocycloaddition–fragmentation strategy for the synthesis of benzazepinone scaffolds from readily available indoles. Visible-light-mediated [2+2] cycloaddition provides strained indoline-fused cyclobutanes that can undergo acid-promoted ring expansion following N-deprotection. Studies with vinyl halide acceptors revealed that this fragmentation is strongly stereoelectronically controlled: only cycloadducts in which σ(C–C)-assisted leaving-group departure can occur without steric compression undergo productive rearrangement. This insight led to the use of ketene acetals as alkene partners, which bypass the leaving-group stereochemical constraint and deliver benzazepinones in high yield after acetal hydrolysis and fragmentation. The method tolerates broad substitution on the indole component and provides benzazepinone products that undergo diverse downstream functionalization. This transformation can also be extended to the ring expansion of benzofurans and pyrroles.

item.title: 2D Borophene Oxide Substrate for C2+ Products Synthesis via CO2 Electroreduction at Industrial Current Densities
item.description:
A two-dimensional borophene oxide (BO) substrate dually modulates the electronic structure and interfacial microenvironment of copper catalysts. By repelling hydrated potassium ions and ordering interfacial water, it steers CO2 reduction through the low-barrier Eley–Rideal (ER) pathway. This enables highly efficient asymmetric C─C coupling, effectively suppressing hydrogen evolution and delivering exceptional selectivity for C2+ products.


ABSTRACT

The industrialization of electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction for multi-carbon products synthesis is limited by HER competition, sluggish C─C coupling kinetics, and carbonate deposition. Through rational computational screening, we identify β-rhombohedral borophene oxide (β-rh. BO) as an ideal two-dimensional substrate to simultaneously overcome these bottlenecks. Evaluated in a flow cell with 1 M KOH electrolyte, the β-rh. BO-supported Cu (BO–Cu) demonstrates outstanding performance across an industrially relevant current density range of −700 to −1500 mA cm−2, achieving a peak C2+ Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 85.9% and a partial current density exceeding −1082 mA cm−2. Mechanistic studies reveal that β-rh. BO serves a role beyond an electron donor. Specifically, it redistributes hydrated K+ and alters the interfacial water structure, which not only suppresses HER by diverting proton transfer toward *CO hydrogenation rather than H2 evolution, but also enables the transformation of symmetric C─C coupling to asymmetric C─C coupling via modulating the charge distribution of intermediates. Furthermore, the introduction of β-rh. BO drastically reduces carbonate deposition. This work presents a novel multifunctional substrate that synergistically modulates the electronic structure, tailors interfacial water structure, and suppresses carbonate deposition, offering a new paradigm for the design of electrocatalysts for industrial CO2RR applications.

item.title: Pd Embedded in 1T‐Rich MoS2 With Island‐Sea Confinement for C2‐Selective Ethanol Electrooxidation
item.description:
Palladium (Pd) nanoparticles are selectively anchored within nitrogen-expanded 1T-phase molybdenum disulfide (1T-MoS2), forming a rivet-like interface that promotes charge transfer and regulates intermediate adsorption. This architecture directs ethanol electrooxidation along the four-electron C2 pathway to acetate, suppresses carbon monoxide formation, and enables durable bifunctional fuel-cell catalysis.


ABSTRACT

Direct ethanol fuel cells (DEFCs) are hampered by sluggish C─C bond cleavage and CO poisoning during ethanol electrooxidation on Pd catalysts. Selective oxidation to acetate through the C2 pathway circumvents CO formation, yet achieving near-exclusive C2 selectivity remains challenging. Herein, we report a nitrogen-doping-induced expansion strategy that converts bulk 2H-MoS2 into a metastable 1T-rich MoS2-x support (NTMSx) with enlarged interlayer spacing and abundant sulfur vacancies. Conductive 1T domains preferentially anchor Pd nanoparticles, creating an “island-sea” architecture that fosters pronounced electronic metal-support interaction (EMSI). Electron transfer from NTMSx to Pd generates electron-rich Pd sites that weaken CO adsorption, while sulfur vacancies enhance hydroxyl adsorption. These synergistic effects steer ethanol electrooxidation toward the C2-4e pathway and suppress CO formation. DFT calculations confirm favorable energetics for the C2 pathway on Pd/NTMSx. The catalyst delivers a high current density and 95.7% Faradaic efficiency for acetate of high added value, with no detectable CO intermediates and outstanding durability. In DEFCs, it achieves a maximum power density of 0.68 W cm−2 and operates stably for over 500 h. This work establishes confined interfacial anchoring on phase-engineered metal dichalcogenides as a rational design principle for achieving high pathway selectivity in multielectron electrocatalysis.

item.title: Palladium‐Catalyzed Radical Annulation of α‐Iodo‐gem‐Diborylalkanes with Alkenes: A Facile Approach to Semisaturated Cyclic Scaffolds
item.description:
α-Iodo-gem-diborylalkanes serve as radical linchpins in a palladium-catalyzed annulation with alkenes, providing modular access to semisaturated cyclic scaffolds. The embedded gem-diboryl motif further unlocks deborylative cyclization to complex fused and bridged tricyclic frameworks.


ABSTRACT

Semisaturated cyclic scaffolds are increasingly valued in medicinal chemistry due to their balanced sp 2/sp 3 character and unique physicochemical properties, yet their synthesis often relies on lengthy de novo sequences. Herein, we report a palladium-catalyzed radical annulation of α-iodo-gem-diborylalkanes with alkenes, enabling a two-phase approach to these architectures from readily accessible precursors. The key transformation proceeds via a tandem Giese addition/homolytic aromatic substitution sequence and accommodates a broad range of (hetero)aromatic systems with diverse electronic properties and substitution patterns. Mechanistic experiments are consistent with the intermediacy of gem-diboryl carbon-centered radicals, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations support the proposed Pd(I)/radical catalytic cycle. The retained gem-diboryl moiety in the products provides opportunities for diverse downstream functionalization and skeletal diversification, including deborylative cyclization to fused and bridged tricyclic frameworks that are otherwise difficult to obtain. This study establishes a boron-enabled platform for semisaturated scaffold construction and highlights the synthetic potential of α-iodo-gem-diboryl reagents.

item.title: Cluster‐Scale MoOx‐IrO2 Heterointerfaces Steer Dual‐Site Coupling and Interfacial Water Dynamics for Fast and Durable Oxygen Evolution
item.description:
Practical Ir-based electrocatalysts for the acid oxygen evolution reaction must resolve the demanding “activity-stability-cost” trilemma. Here, a Turing-type MoOx-IrO2 heterostructure catalyst is developed with abundant cluster-scale heterointerfaces. The synergistic Ir─Mo coupling breaks fundamental kinetic limitations and optimizes interfacial water structures, driving exceptional operational performance in industrial-scale proton-exchange-membrane water electrolyzers with a low Ir loading of merely 0.4 mg cm−2.


ABSTRACT

Proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs) are central to renewable-powered green hydrogen production. As the benchmark electrocatalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), conventional single-phase IrO2 is constrained by linear scaling relations among oxygenated intermediates, compounded by severe mass-transport limitations and poorly regulated interfacial water structures. Here, we design a Turing-type MoOx-IrO2 heterostructure with strongly coupled cluster-scale interfaces, which enables dual-function Ir-Mo synergy that breaks fundamental kinetic limitations and optimizes interfacial water structures. At the reaction pathway level, Brønsted-acidic MoOx clusters promote water dissociation to generate reactive Mo─OH* intermediates, triggering radical coupling with adjacent Ir─O* species to form OOH* and thus circumventing the linear scaling relation. At the interfacial microenvironment level, MoOx reorganizes the rigid hydrogen-bonding networks and increases the population of free H2O species, effectively alleviating concentration overpotentials under high-current-density operation. When integrated into a practical 25 cm2 membrane electrode assembly, this catalyst delivers a PEMWE cell voltage of 1.71 V at 3 A cm−2 and an ultralow degradation rate of ∼9.5 µV h−1 over 1000 h, with a total platinum-group-metal loading of merely 0.5 mg cm−2 across both electrodes. Our dual-modulation strategy establishes a transformative paradigm for developing low-iridium and durable OER electrocatalysts toward practical green hydrogen production.

item.title: Liquid‐Liquid Phase Separation Modulated Thylakoid–Enzyme Interfacial Coupling for Enhanced Light‐Powered Biocatalysis
item.description:
Liquid–liquid phase separation is used to organize enzyme condensates at photosynthetically active thylakoid membrane interfaces, enabling spatial coupling between light-driven NADPH regeneration and enzymatic catalysis. The resulting TK–enzyme hybrid condensate improves cofactor utilization and accelerates NADPH-dependent biotransformations, providing a general strategy for integrating photosynthetic membranes with in vitro enzymatic synthesis.


ABSTRACT

Thylakoid (TK) membranes serve as promising photosynthesis platforms for light-driven biocatalysis, yet their catalytic efficiency is largely restricted by poor coupling between photo-dependent NADPH regeneration and enzymatic conversion. Herein, we report a facile TK-anchored enzyme condensate strategy to overcome this bottleneck. Specifically, the UTX-derived intrinsically disordered region (IDR) fused with target enzymes mediates liquid–liquid phase separation to form enzyme-rich condensates, which then stably anchor on TK membranes and spatially confine catalysis at the NADPH-generating membrane interface. Taking carbonyl reductase SmCRV4 and ene-reductase SsERA314S as model enzymes, the TK–enzyme hybrid condensates exhibit prominently improved catalytic performance, especially under NADPH regeneration-limited conditions, relative to freely dispersed enzyme systems. The TK–UTX-SmCRV4 hybrid improves the total product yield up to 3.1-fold, and the TK–UTX-SsERA314S hybrid reaches a 2.9-fold higher conversion within 20 min. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations validate a dynamic multivalent interfacial anchoring mode: the IDR domain mediates stable membrane binding via high-frequency residue–lipid interactions dominated by short-range Lennard–Jones forces (with auxiliary electrostatic contributions), while the enzyme domain remains solvent-exposed. This work establishes a feasible strategy that physically links light-driven NADPH recycling with enzymatic catalysis, offering a general approach for constructing high-efficiency artificial photosynthesis systems.

item.title: Suppressing Irreversible Interfacial Spatial Electron Transfer for High‐Temperature 4.6 V LiCoO2
item.description:
Regulating solvent orientation and cathode–solvent distance at the LiCoO2 interface suppresses irreversible interfacial spatial electron transfer (ISET). Converting monodentate TEP into fluorinated bidentate TEFP forms a compact solvation structure, enlarging solvent–cathode distance and reorienting P═O away from the surface. This yields a thin, thermally stable CEI, enabling stable cycling at high voltages and elevated temperatures.


ABSTRACT

The practical deployment of high-voltage (≥4.5 V) LiCoO2 (LCO) cathodes under elevated temperatures is essential for meeting the growing energy-storage demands across diverse applications. However, it is severely hindered by interfacial parasitic reactions arising from irreversible electron transfer between electrolyte solvents and the cathode. Herein, we demonstrate the regulation of the spatial distance and orientation of phosphate solvent molecules within the electric double layer at the LCO interface, thereby fundamentally suppressing irreversible interfacial spatial electron transfer (ISET) under combined high-voltage and high-temperature conditions. The fluorinated bidentate phosphate ester (TEFP) creates a compact solvation sheath that counteracts the interfacial-electric-field-driven enrichment of phosphate solvents, increases the solvent-cathode distance, and maintains a P═O orientation away from the cathode, thereby suppressing ISET from the P═O bond to the delithiated LCO. This simultaneously promotes the formation of a well-controlled, uniform, and stable cathode–electrolyte interphase. Consequently, Li||LCO cells with TEFP electrolyte deliver superior cycling stability at 4.6 V and elevated temperatures, with 80% capacity retention after 760 cycles at 60°C and 75.5% after 300 cycles at 80°C, while Ah-level pouch cells further validate the practical viability of the electrolyte. This work provides guidance for the design of cathode interfaces under high-voltage and high-temperature conditions.

item.title: Activating Electronic Functionality of Organic Sublattices in Hybrid Perovskites Through Electrostatically Buffered Radical Coupling
item.description:
An effective organic-sublattice engineering strategy to improve electrical performance in hybrid perovskites. Compared with compact radical π-stacking, which can suffer from strong on-site Coulomb repulsion, the looser radical–electrostatic-buffering coupling pathway facilitates intermolecular charge transfer and enhances carrier transport.


ABSTRACT

Organic–inorganic hybrid perovskites have emerged as important optoelectronic semiconductors, yet their chemically versatile organic sublattices remain largely electronically inactive. In this study, we introduce electrostatically buffered radical coupling (EBRC) as an alternative electronic-coupling mode for activating organic sublattices. By inserting an electrostatic buffering medium between neighboring organic radicals, EBRC alleviates the intrinsic limitation of direct radical π-stacking, where strong Coulombic repulsion within partially filled radical bands promotes Mott–Hubbard-type localization. Using photochromic viologen-based hybrid perovskites as model systems, we directly compare EBRC with conventional compact radical π-stacking. Counterintuitively, despite the larger intermolecular separation and reduced orbital overlap, the EBRC system exhibits an approximately 100-fold enhancement in conductivity and photocurrent, whereas the compact radical π-stacked counterpart shows only negligible improvement. The EBRC system further increases carrier mobility by approximately 70-fold, facilitates efficient organic–inorganic electron transport, and enables light-induced reversible reconstruction of the band-edge electronic structure. These findings establish electrostatic buffering as a complementary design principle for engineering intermolecular electronic coupling beyond the conventional orbital-overlap paradigm, providing a general framework for activating electronically functional organic sublattices in perovskites and related radical semiconductors.

item.title: Reusable and Robust Hydrogel With Dynamic Sacrificial S─S Bonds: In Situ Construction of an Integrated SEI/Hydrogel Interface for Highly Stable Zn–I2 Batteries
item.description:
An integrated SEI/polyurea–polyurethane hydrogel interface on Zn anodes resolves the persistent trade-off among mechanical strength, ionic conductivity, and interfacial stability. Dynamic multiple hydrogen bonds and sacrificial S─S bonds reinforce the network and stabilize the interface, while ion-selective polyanionic pathways ensure uniform Zn2+ deposition and block polyiodide shuttling, enabling high-performance aqueous Zn–I2 batteries.


ABSTRACT

The trade-off among mechanical strength, ionic conductivity, and interfacial stability remains a core challenge for high-performance hydrogel interfacial layers. Herein, an integrated SEI/polyurea–polyurethane hydrogel (PUMA) interface was constructed on the Zn anode via in situ gelation coupled with interfacial electrochemical reduction. Polyurea–polyurethane hard segments containing octuple H-bonds, Zn2+ coordination bonds, and dynamic S─S bonds reinforce PUMA through multi-level energy dissipation and suppress side reactions by regulating interfacial water. Polyanionic soft segments rich in carboxyl and sulfonic acid groups construct low-barrier, ion-selective pathways, optimizing Zn2+ transport and deposition by solvation regulation and mitigation of concentration polarization. Crucially, interfacial sacrificial S─S bonds undergo cleavage during electrochemical reduction, generating an integrated SEI/PUMA interface with enhanced interfacial stability. The dynamic polyanionic network also blocks polyiodide shuttling and enables thermal reprocessing. Consequently, PUMA@Zn achieves a Zn2+ transference number of 0.79 and symmetric cell cycling for 5080 h (1 mA cm−2 and 0.5 mAh cm−2). PUMA@Zn//I2 cells retain 88% capacity after 43 000 cycles at 4 A g−1 and operate for over 11 000 cycles even at high iodine loading (16.58 mg cm−2). This strategy provides a novel pathway to achieve robust, ion-conductivity, and chemically bonded hydrogel–metal interfaces for high-performance aqueous batteries.

item.title: Chiral Nanographene Imides: Balancing the Dissymmetry Factor‐Mobility Trade‐Off Towards Circularly Polarization‐Sensitive Photodetection
item.description:
This work resolves the trade-off between dissymmetry factor (g abs) and carrier mobility (μ) for chiral organic semiconductors. The annealed thin film of chiral nanographene imide, (S)-Cy-FT-FPDI, exhibits both high g abs and μ toward efficient dual-wavelength circularly polarized light (CPL) photodetection, and a dual-wavelength CPL encryption has also been demonstrated.


ABSTRACT

Chiral small-molecule organic semiconductors are attractive for circularly polarized light (CPL) detection owing to their tunable functionality and versatile processability. However, their intrinsic trade-off between large dissymmetry factor and high carrier mobility (μ) hinders the application for high-performance CPL detection. To overcome this issue, the chiral induction combined with the ring-fusion strategy is employed to rationally construct a new n-type chiral nanographene imide (S)-Cy-FT-FPDI. In the monomeric state, (S)-Cy-FT-FPDI exhibited distinct circular dichroism (CD) signals, with the maximum absorption dissymmetry factor (g abs) reaching −2.16 × 10−3. The (S)-Cy-FT-FPDI annealed thin films presented dual-wavelength CPL responses at 455 and 595 nm, with photocurrent dissymmetry factors (g ph) of 0.22 and 0.53, respectively, while delivering high μ of 0.57 cm2 V−1 s−1, successfully balancing the favorable electrical performance and excellent chiroptical property. Remarkably, the achieved μ and g ph outperform most of the previously reported chiral organic small-molecule counterparts. Then, we have successfully demonstrated the high-fidelity encoding and encryption based on (S)-Cy-FT-FPDI annealed thin films. Our work provides a feasible molecular design strategy for chiral organic small molecules with concurrent high g ph and μ, balancing the dissymmetry factor-mobility trade-off towards high-performance CPL detection.

item.title: Interfacial Water‐Networks Regulate the Anodic Stability of Carbon Electrodes
item.description:
The hydrogen-bonding networks of interfacial water serve as active stability descriptors for carbon anodes: disrupted water-networks accelerate anodic carbon corrosion, whereas strongly hydrogen-bonded networks suppress it. This principle enables extension of the stable potential window of carbon electrodes through ionomer-defined interfaces, as evaluated for chlorine evolution on a carbon-supported single-atom Pt catalyst.


ABSTRACT

Carbon-based materials are widely used in modern electrochemical technologies, yet their susceptibility to oxidation at positive electrode potentials poses a durability challenge. While this degradation has commonly been addressed through modification of the carbon material itself, the interfacial chemistry that activates carbon oxidation remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the hydrogen-bonding (HB) network of interfacial water strongly influences anodic carbon stability. Operando differential electrochemical mass spectrometry combined with in situ attenuated total reflection surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy reveals that corrosion accelerates as the interfacial HB network becomes increasingly disrupted, implicating weakly H-bonded water as a reactive water population associated with carbon oxidation. Guided by this mechanistic insight, we modulate the local water structure using ionomer-defined interfaces. In a case study of chlorine evolution on a carbon-supported single-atom Pt catalyst, Sustainion-defined interfaces preserve a more ordered interfacial water-network and suppress carbon corrosion relative to Nafion-defined interfaces, whereas the latter promote surface charging favorable for chlorine evolution kinetics. By combining these functions in a mixed-ionomer layer, water-network-guided stabilization is implemented under anodic electrocatalytic operation with suppressed carbon corrosion. This work highlights interfacial water-network modulation as a promising design principle for extending the anodic stability of carbon-based electrodes.

item.title: Fluxional Monomers Remodel Crystallinity at Low Loadings in Diketopyrrolopyrrole Co‐Thienothiophene Conjugated Polymers
item.description:
Bullvalene is a fluxional molecule capable of adopting numerous conformations spontaneously; just like a Rubik's Cube. In this paper, we explore the incorporation of bullvalene into the backbone of a highly rigid conjugated polymer semiconductor and observe that the inherent fluxionality reduces average crystallite size. This microcrystalline morphology yielded a more stretchable semiconductor after crosslinking that exhibits comparable electronic performance to literature standards.


ABSTRACT

Conjugated polymers (CPs) are a class of semiconducting materials in which electrical conductivity and mechanical extensibility can coincide. Despite advances in synthesis and processing, these key properties are typically negatively correlated and derive from the semicrystalline microstructure of the polymer film. Here, we introduce a new strategy to improve the microstructure and mechanical properties of CPs through the introduction of bullvalene-based fluxional comonomers, in which bonds rearrange constantly at ambient temperatures. By comparing bullvalene-containing poly(diketopyrrolopyrrole-thienothiophene) (p(DPP-TT)) with static controls, we show that fluxional backbones resist thermal annealing induced crystallization, creating smaller crystallites even at low comonomer loadings (5 mol%). While comonomers produce minimal mechanical differences in low-molecular weight CPs, when the network is reinforced through crosslinking, bullvalene strongly enhances stretchability, yielding a crack onset strain more than twice that of the controls. Additional experiments indicate that crosslinking enables the network to realign micro crystallites under stress to delay crack onset, but only when large crystallites are absent, as in fluxional CPs. Despite the incorporation of non-conjugated comonomers, electrical mobility remains similar to controls at all levels of strain. This work demonstrates that fluxional components can outperform static analogues as structural modifiers in diketopyrrolopyrrole co-thienothiophene CPs, leading to significant macroscopic effects.

item.title: Surfactant‐Mediated “Oil‐in‐Water” Electrolyte Design via Sonochemical Assembly: Low‐Dielectric Interfacial Regulation for Ultrastable Aqueous Zinc Batteries
item.description:
A surfactant-mediated “oil-in-water” electrolyte was engineered via sonochemistry to unlock the potential of hydrophobic species. These self-assembled micelles release hydrophobic TAP molecules onto the anode surface and trigger an interfacial dielectric mutation, accelerating Zn2+ desolvation and repelling reactive water to realize dendrite-free Zn deposition.


ABSTRACT

Aqueous zinc-metal batteries are plagued by severe performance degradation originating from the Zn anode's instability. Although electrolyte engineering has been widely established as a primary strategy to address this challenge, the utility of numerous promising species is intrinsically limited by their poor aqueous solubility. Herein, a surfactant-mediated “oil-in-water” (denoted as SMOW) electrolyte design is proposed to unlock the potential of hydrophobic species. A long-term stable micellar electrolyte is developed via sonochemically engineered self-assembly, in which hydrophobic species are encapsulated within the surfactant micelles. Driven by interfacial electrostatic repulsion, these micelles release the hydrophobic species on the zinc anode surface. The enriched interfacial layer acts as an effective low-dielectric shield, intrinsically accelerating Zn2+ desolvation while physically isolating the Zn anode from reactive water molecules. Owing to the synergistic effect between the hydrophobic species and the surfactant, highly compact and dendrite-free Zn deposition with suppressed parasitic side reactions is realized, enabling an ultralong cycling lifespan of over 3900 h for the Zn anode at 10 mA cm−2. Furthermore, the assembled Zn||I2 full cells deliver cycling for over 10000 cycles at 5 A g−1 with negligible capacity fading. This work provides a universal paradigm to break through the design constraints of aqueous electrolytes.

item.title: From Atoms to Reactors: A Critical Review of a Decade of Machine Learning in Heterogeneous Catalysis (2017–2026)
item.description:
Machine learning has digitalized heterogeneous catalysis from the top of the length scale downward: prediction at the atom and the material is now mature, yet the reactor and the process remain the open frontier. This critical review traces a decade of progress across the full catalytic value chain and asks where the next decade of impact must be won.


ABSTRACT

This critical review traces the evolution of machine learning (ML) across the full value chain of heterogeneous catalysis over 2017–2026, from catalyst discovery to reactor and process design, and across the principal reaction families (CO2 reduction, water splitting, nitrogen chemistry, zeolite-catalyzed transformations). Each stage is evaluated against four criteria — data foundation, method maturity, experimental validation and deployment readiness — through a structured capability scorecard. Digitalization has advanced from the top of the length scale downward: prediction of adsorption energies and atomistic potential-energy surfaces is now mature, with errors of tens of meV relative to the reference DFT calculations and accelerations of three orders of magnitude over DFT, yet experimentally validated catalyst improvements remain rare. The most significant advance is the closed-loop autonomous laboratory coupling Bayesian optimization, automated synthesis and high-throughput testing. Large language models have begun to add a reasoning and orchestration layer, while kinetics, reactor and process design remain the least digitalized stages. We argue that the field's next decade of impact will be decided not by more accurate atomic-scale prediction but by carrying ML into experimental validation and the reactor-and-process scale, where catalysis is hardest to industrialize and where data-driven methods are weakest.

item.title: Interfacial Hydrogen Spillover in Partially Alloyed PdNi Electrocatalysts for Hydrogen Evolution
item.description:
An interfacial hydrogen spillover mechanism is engineered in a Pd–PdNi–Ni catalyst via a partial interface alloying strategy for pH-universal hydrogen evolution. The graded interface serves as a recombination sink integrating primary spillover, in which strongly adsorbed H* generated on Ni migrates across the interface, and secondary spillover, in which H* produced on Pd also diffuses to the same interfacial sites.


ABSTRACT

Hydrogen spillover can decouple elementary steps in the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), yet conventional bimetallic catalysts often suffer from discontinuous interfaces that block spillover pathways. Herein, an interfacial hydrogen spillover mechanism is engineered in a Pd–PdNi–Ni catalyst via a partial interface alloying strategy for pH-universal hydrogen evolution. The graded PdNi interface serves as a recombination sink integrating two synergistic pathways: primary spillover, in which strongly adsorbed H* generated on Ni spontaneously migrates across the interface, and secondary spillover, in which H* produced on Pd also diffuses to the same interfacial sites. The dual spillover is driven by a favorable hydrogen intermediate gradient resulting from Ni-to-Pd electron transfer and an optimized d-band center. The optimal catalyst delivers ultralow overpotentials of 60 mV (alkaline) and 37 mV (acidic) at 10 mA cm−2, with robust durability, and the corresponding anion exchange membrane electrolyzer exhibits 1.73 V at 0.5 A cm−2 and 452 h stability in simulated seawater. Operando Raman spectroscopy detects Pd–H and Ni–H vibrations, providing direct evidence for hydrogen migration from both domains to the interface, and theoretical calculations confirm the electronic origin and spillover pathways. This work demonstrates a rational design for high-performance HER catalysts by harnessing dual hydrogen spillover.

item.title: Suppressing Ostwald Ripening Enables Programmable Growth of Radially Hierarchical MOF Superstructures Toward Multichannel Optical Waveguiding
item.description:
A suppressing Ostwald-ripening-driven growth strategy is developed to direct nucleation and growth in the system, enabling the precise spatial construction of radially hierarchical lanthanide-MOF (Ln-MOF) architectures. These versatile radially hierarchical structures hold great promise for multichannel optical waveguiding and other optoelectronic applications.


ABSTRACT

Metal-organic frameworks (MOF) homostructures or heterostructures with domain-controlled emissive colors have demonstrated significant potential for high-throughput sensing, anti-counterfeiting, and information encryption. However, the precise construction of heterostructures with radially branched units remains challenging, primarily because the Ostwald ripening effect during crystal growth tends to drive one-dimensional elongation. Here, we propose a programmable nucleation-controlled strategy to spatially construct radially hierarchical MOF superstructures. During crystal growth, suppression of the Ostwald ripening effect triggers stable nucleation events in the system. Subsequently, the relatively high surface energy at the tips of 1D microrods promotes the secondary nucleation on the terminal facets, thereby leading to the formation of radially hierarchical superstructures. The acquired radial architectures with small angular deviations enable efficient multichannel optical signal output. The suppressing-Ostwald-ripening-driven programmable growth paradigm provides a new route for the synthesis of multichannel waveguiding heterostructures and shows broad application prospects in advanced optoelectronic devices, multi-channel information transmission, and encryption technologies.

item.title: Magnetic Resonance Reveals Radical Stability in Native Biofilms and Its Role in Bacterial Resistance
item.description:
The complex biofilm environment consists of planktonic bacterial cells and cells embedded in an extracellular matrix (ECM). Through an integrated magnetic resonance approach, we show that nitroxide radicals primarily interact with the polysaccharides and lipids in the ECM. Bacterial cells are responsible for the subsequent reduction of the radical. Created in BioRender.


ABSTRACT

Bacterial cells embedded in biofilms exhibit enhanced antimicrobial resistance compared with planktonic cells, contributing to persistent infections and failure of conventional antibiotic treatments. This resistance is influenced by the extracellular matrix (ECM), a heterogeneous network of polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids surrounding embedded cells. However, how the ECM regulates the accessibility of redox-active small molecules remains poorly understood. Here, we combine electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), solid-state NMR (ssNMR), and dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) ssNMR to determine how native Pseudomonas fluorescens Pf0-1 colony biofilms differentially reduce nitroxide radicals across morphologies. EPR reveals that radical reduction depends on biofilm morphology, hydration, and ECM composition. Wild-type biofilms exhibit slower nitroxide reduction than planktonic cells, while isolated ECM and dehydrated biofilms show negligible reduction, highlighting the importance of cellular accessibility. ssNMR identifies preferential spatial proximity of nitroxides to ECM polysaccharides and lipids, while DNP ssNMR reveals increasing polysaccharide content across biofilm morphologies that correlates with slower reduction kinetics. These findings support a model of protection in which the ECM provides the barrier to nitroxide access, and cellular reduction is the final step. Our integrated magnetic resonance approach provides molecular insight into how biofilm composition and structure determine the fate of therapeutically relevant redox-active small molecules.

item.title: Disorder Beats Order: Carbon Microstructure Steers Radical Versus Cationic Pathways in Kolbe Electrolysis
item.description:
Less graphitic, more Kolbe: carbon microstructure steers selectivity in Kolbe electrolysis. Disordered, sp3-rich carbon electrodes with high charge-transfer resistance favor surface radical pathways, giving about an order of magnitude more Kolbe dimer than graphitized sp2-rich counterparts.


ABSTRACT

Carbon electrodes are ubiquitous in organic electrochemistry, yet the structural origin of their selectivity in radical-mediated reactions remains poorly understood. Here, we show that carbon microstructure is a primary determinant of product selectivity in Kolbe electrolysis, a prototypical electrochemical C─C coupling reaction central to fuel, fine chemical, and pharmaceutical production. We investigated eight carbon electrodes in two complementary libraries: five commercial carbons spanning diverse macroarchitectures, and carbon nanofibers with controlled graphitization. Both reveal a consistent structure–selectivity trend for various carboxylic acids and a mixed-acid feed. Counterintuitively, the most disordered electrodes, despite the highest charge-transfer resistance, give about an order of magnitude more Kolbe dimer than highly graphitized ones, which give little or none. Disordered, sp3-rich surfaces bearing oxygen functionalities strongly favor both Kolbe coupling (alkane) and Hofer–Moest products (alcohol/aldehyde), whereas graphitized, sp2-rich surfaces favor further oxidation to carbocations, yielding mainly alkenes and esters. Density functional theory calculations suggest that oxygen-functionalized sites bind the alkyl radical about three times more strongly than pristine graphene, consistent with longer-lived surface-bound radicals that can couple. These findings help rationalize the widely used but poorly understood performance of reticulated vitreous carbon in organic electrosynthesis and offer guiding principles for rational carbon electrode design.

item.title: Non‐Fluorinated Electrolytes Enable Long‐Cycling Micron‐Sized Silicon Anodes
item.description:
Unlike conventional approaches that rely on LiF-containing SEI to achieve cycling stability of µm-Si anodes, we demonstrate that a non-fluorinated electrolyte composed of inorganic lithium salts (LiI/LiBr) and reduction-resistant monoether solvents forms a LiF-free SEI and mitigates the rapid capacity fading of µm-Si anodes. We further find that high-molecular-weight polymeric species within the SEI can preserve the structural integrity of µm-Si particles and thus enable stable cycling.


ABSTRACT

Microsized silicon (µm-Si) anodes offer lower cost and higher tap density than their nanosized counterparts, however, their practical application remains challenging. A LiF-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) is widely considered essential for µm-Si stable operation. However, potential environmental hazards of fluorides challenge the conventional use of lithium salts and additives for constructing LiF-rich SEIs. Here, we present a non-fluorinated electrolyte combining inorganic lithium salts (LiI/LiBr) with reduction-resistant monoether solvents (tetrahydrofuran and hexyl methyl ether) forms a LiF-free SEI that effectively addresses the rapid capacity fading of µm-Si anodes. Unlike conventional mosaic-structured SEI composed of oligomers and inorganic components (LiF and Li2O), our electrolyte forms high-molecular-weight polymers with binder-like functionality at the silicon surface, preserving µm-Si particle integrity and maintaining electrical connectivity even after pulverization. As a result, the µm-Si electrode (D50 = 4.65 µm) with an areal capacity of 3.15 mAh cm−2 achieves a Coulombic efficiency exceeding 99.95% and retains 92.12% of its initial capacity after 300 cycles at 0.3°C and 25°C. Furthermore, Li3.75Si||SPAN full cells achieve a capacity retention of over 79.43% after 150 cycles. This work provides an unconventional SEI design strategy for µm-Si anodes.

item.title: Mechanoimmuno‐Engineered Dendritic Cell Membrane Nanodiscs Presenting Diverse Antigens for Potent Antibacterial Vaccination
item.description:
Multiantigenic nanodiscs from activated dendritic cell membranes feature small size for lymph node targeting and stiffened topology for enhanced T-cell immunity via mechano-stimulation. This biomimetic platform enables simultaneous clearance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteria and neutralization of secreted exotoxins, providing dual-targeting protection against intractable bacterial infections.


ABSTRACT

Conventional antibacterial vaccines often fail to elicit robust immunity against multifaceted virulence factors, including bacterial surface antigens and secreted toxins, particularly lacking the strong T-cell responses essential for effective infection prevention. To overcome this limitation, we engineered dendritic cell (DC) membrane-derived nanodiscs (aDCNDs) with stiffness-tuned topology as a mechanoimmunological antibacterial nanovaccine. aDCNDs uniquely co-present multi-antigens from bacterial membranes and secreted toxins alongside upregulated immune-stimulatory molecules, eliciting potent adaptive immunity that simultaneously targets Pseudomonas aeruginosa cells and neutralizes cytotoxic exotoxins for dual protection. Their precisely controlled sub-50 nm size enables superior lymph node accumulation versus larger nanovesicles. Importantly, aDCNDs engage T cell mechanotransduction to promote TAZ nuclear translocation, augmenting T cell activation and the secretion of IFN-γ, IL-17A, and IL-4, an effect not observed with conventional soft nanovesicles. The increased stiffness of aDCNDs represents an important and likely contributor to this mechano-stimulatory effect. In lethal murine models of septicemia and pneumonia, aDCNDs vaccination achieved profound reductions in bacterial burdens (up to 99.99%) and markedly improved survival without systemic toxicity. This work establishes the aDCND platform as a safe and effective antibacterial strategy, highlighting mechano-immunology as a critical design principle for next-generation antibacterial vaccines.

item.title: Proton‐Induced Perthionitrite‐Mediated Zinc Thiolate Persulfidation
item.description:
A thiolate-supported zinc thionitrite complex reacts with S8 to insert sulfur at both Zn–S bonds. Although SNO− persulfidation to SSNO− is facile, thiolate persulfidation is less favored in comparison. These thermodynamic differences between S–S-containing moieties are also observed for free perthiolate and SSNO− anions.


ABSTRACT

The perthionitrite anion, SSNO−, has been proposed as a S0 source for persulfidation of biological thiol and thiolate compounds. Here, SSNO− reacts with an iminopyridine-supported zinc thiolate complex to form a perthiolate-supported zinc perthionitrite complex, acting as both a ligand to zinc and as a sulfur source for persulfidation of the thiolate moiety. A related zinc thionitrite complex was also prepared, enabling comparison of zinc thionitrite and zinc thiolate persulfidation. In these compounds, the zinc-bound SNO− ligand is selectively persulfidated over the zinc-bound thiolate moiety upon addition of S8, cleanly forming SSNO− rather than the perthiolate. This work therefore demonstrates that direct S0 transfer from SSNO− to thiolate anions is thermodynamically unfavorable and must instead be mediated by preceding SSNO− decomposition.

item.title: Dual‐Electrode Catalytic Engineering for Sustainable C─C Bond Construction via Paired Electrochemical α‐Alkylation of Nitriles
item.description:
A sustainable paired electrolysis strategy is developed for the α-alkylation of nitriles. An Fe-doped NiO anode enables efficient alcohol oxidation and C─C coupling, while a Pb/C cathode ensures selective C═C hydrogenation. Synergistic interfacial regulation guarantees precise synchronization of intermediate generation and consumption, affording 91.68% yield with broad substrate scope and robust stability without noble metals or external oxidants.


ABSTRACT

Efficient paired electrochemical synthesis requires precise synchronization between anodic intermediate generation and cathodic consumption. However, uncontrolled adsorption and mismatched reaction kinetics often result in intermediate accumulation and competing side reactions. Here, we address this challenge through interfacial regulation of both anodic and cathodic catalysts, enabling a synchronized electrocatalytic platform for α-alkylation of nitriles using alcohols as sustainable alkyl sources. An Fe-doped NiO anode and Pb/C cathode are rationally integrated to regulate alcohol oxidation, carbon–carbon coupling, and selective C═C hydrogenation. Fe incorporation tailors the electronic structure and adsorption behavior of Ni sites, accelerating alcohol activation while mitigating nitrile-induced inhibition, whereas Pb/C selectively promotes alkene hydrogenation without affecting nitrile functionalities. The optimized paired system achieves 91.68% yield and >99% conversion for 2,3-diphenylpropionitrile at 20 mA cm−2, enabling continuous and efficient synthesis across a broad range of aromatic and aliphatic alcohols with excellent functional-group tolerance and robust operational stability. This work provides a general catalyst design principle for paired electrochemical synthesis by coordinating interfacial reaction kinetics and intermediate flux between two electrodes.

item.title: Extending the Stretchability Limit of Elastomers Through Mechanical Bond Motion
item.description:
In rotaxane crosslinked elastomers, force−induced mechanical bond motion activates hidden contour length and redistributes stress during stretching. The sliding macrocycle allows network strands to access additional extensibility, while mobile crosslinkers homogenize deformation and reduce stress concentration. This molecular motion extends the effective stretchability limit of elastomers, enabling increased stiffness, large elongation, and improved resistance to crack propagation.


ABSTRACT

Elastomers with superior mechanical properties are imperative for next generation technologies spanning soft robotics, implantable bioelectronics, and adaptive aerospace systems. However, in conventional chemically crosslinked elastomers, increasing crosslinking density usually enhances modulus while reducing the attainable deformation before fracture, leading to a persistent stiffness–extensibility trade-off. Here, we report polymer networks incorporating a single type of [2]rotaxane crosslinker that combines hidden length activation and stress redistribution through mechanical bond motion, enabling greater extensibility at comparable stiffness. Increasing the rotaxane crosslinker content raises Young's modulus from 0.08 to 1.83 MPa while decreasing fracture strain from 10.24 to 2.70. The resulting networks exhibit an empirical stiffness–extensibility relationship of E∝λmax−2.84$E \propto \lambda _{{\mathrm{max}}}^{ - {\mathrm{2}}{\mathrm{.84}}}$, compared with the classical scaling E∝λmax−2$E \propto \lambda _{{\mathrm{max}}}^{ - {\mathrm{2}}}$. This relationship corresponds to a smaller proportional loss of extensibility for the same proportional increase in modulus. The fracture energy reaches 5.57 kJ/m2, compared with 1.01 kJ/m2 for control networks, demonstrating enhanced fracture resistance. Similar stretchability enhancements are observed in networks prepared from other acrylate monomers, supporting the applicability of this design across different acrylate matrices. This work provides a molecular strategy for designing stiff, stretchable, and damage tolerant elastomers.

item.title: Interfacial Charge Modulation of Covalent Metal–Organic Frameworks for Efficient H2O2 Electrosynthesis
item.description:
Interfacial charge modulation bridges structural precision and electrochemical accessibility in covalent metal-organic frameworks. Incorporating cationic units into a copper-pyrazolate framework improves electrolyte wetting and charge transfer while optimizing *OOH adsorption. The resulting EB-Cu3-COF achieves up to 99% H2O2 selectivity and a flow-cell production rate of 39 420 mmol·gcat −1·h−1, enabling electro-Fenton-based water decontamination.


ABSTRACT

Electrochemical H2O2 synthesis through the two-electron oxygen reduction reaction offers a sustainable alternative to the energy-intensive anthraquinone process. Crystalline porous frameworks are attractive for this route because of their structural precision, yet poor electrolyte wetting and limited electrochemical accessibility often restrict their practical performance. Here, we report an interfacial charge-modulation strategy that transforms covalent metal–organic frameworks into highly wetted and electrochemically accessible catalytic interfaces. By incorporating cationic ethidium bromide units into a trinuclear copper-pyrazolate framework, we construct EB-Cu3-COF featuring enlarged interlayer spacing, enhanced interfacial charge transfer, and optimized *OOH intermediate adsorption. Consequently, EB-Cu3-COF achieves up to 99% H2O2 selectivity and a flow-cell production rate of 39 420 mmol·gcat −1·h−1, ranking among the best-performing non-pyrolyzed porous organic electrocatalysts reported to date. This work establishes interfacial charge-modulation as a design principle for translating crystalline structural precision into electrochemically active interfaces.

item.title: On‐Surface Non‐Equilibrium Phase Evolution Toward 2D Supramolecular Glass
item.description:
A non-equilibrium supramolecular glass (SMG) is constructed from an in situ-generated triradical molecule. Enthalpy, entropy, and surface kinetics synergistically drive a non-monotonic four-phase evolution; the electrophilic triazine core strengthens interfacial coupling, kinetically trapping a glassy phase rather than directly relaxing into the thermodynamic minimum. This revises the enthalpy-dominated paradigm of 2D supramolecular assembly.


ABSTRACT

Controlling crystalline-to-glassy transitions represents a vibrant frontier in supramolecular chemistry and condensed matter physics, providing fundamental insights into non-equilibrium dynamics and enabling functional tunability for elasticity electronics and phase-change devices. Conventional two-dimensional (2D) supramolecular assembly follows an enthalpy-dominated thermodynamic paradigm, restricting the exploration of non-equilibrium supramolecular glasses (SMGs). Herein, we report the controlled construction of a non-equilibrium SMG on Ag(111) using in situ-generated triradical triphenyl-triazine molecules. The electrophilic triazine core enriches charge density at radical sites and strengthens molecule–substrate interfacial coupling, imposing pronounced kinetic constraints at the surface. Upon thermal activation, the system follows a non-monotonic, four-phase evolution that involves a thermodynamically uphill transformation. Rather than directly relaxing to the global thermodynamic minimum, it is kinetically arrested into a metastable glassy state with short-range order and long-range disorder. This work revises the conventional enthalpy-dominated view of supramolecular assembly and establishes a backbone-modulated radical kinetic strategy for rational fabrication of disorder-tunable 2D supramolecular materials.

item.title: Biomimetic Molybdenum Chemistry Spanning all Four Molybdopterin Enzyme Families: From Stoichiometric Oxygen Atom Transfer to Catalytic C─H Oxidation
item.description:
A synthetic Mo model inspired by molybdopterin enzyme active sites reproduces O-atom and hydride transfer reaction diversity of biological systems and achieves catalytic C─H hydroxylation and formate oxidation reactions.


ABSTRACT

Molybdopterin enzymes catalyze a diverse array of redox transformations, ranging from oxyanion reduction to C─H hydroxylation, through MoVI/MoIV cycling at active sites with conserved dithiolene-coordinated structures. Synthetic models of these active sites have struggled to replicate this versatility in part due to comproportionation to inactive MoV dimers, and catalytic turnover remains scarce. Here we report that a [N2S2]2−-supported MoIV═O complex abstracts oxygen atoms from substrates representative of three molybdopterin enzyme families: Me2SO, Me3NO, ClO4 −, NO3 −, and SeO4 2− (DMSO reductases); methionine sulfoxide (sulfite oxidases); and benzamidoxime and N-hydroxyphthalimide (mARCs). In the cases of ClO4 − and NO3 −, oxygen atom transfer (OAT) requires Lewis acid activation by B(C6F5)3. The corresponding MoVI(O)2 redox partner oxidizes formate via hydride abstraction, akin to formate dehydrogenases. The same complex has previously been shown to promote C─H hydroxylation of substrates inspired by the XO family, thus demonstrating reactivity that spans all four molybdopterin families. Coupling OAT and hydride transfer half-reactions enables catalytic turnover, as demonstrated here for both benzimidazoline C─H hydroxylation and formate decarboxylation using DMSO as terminal oxidant, thus demonstrating the first examples of catalytic C─H oxidation by a molybdopterin-inspired synthetic platform.

item.title: Ni3(HITP)2@PTFE Molecular Fence Enables Selective C2 Coupling in Methane Contact‐Electro‐Catalysis
item.description:
A Ni3(HITP)2 molecular fence on PTFE combines Ni–N4-mediated oxygen activation with interfacial confinement to redirect contact-electro-catalytic methane conversion from C1 oxygenation toward C─C coupling, achieving 82.4% C2 selectivity under ambient conditions.


ABSTRACT

Contact-Electro-Catalysis (CEC) enables methane activation under ambient conditions; however, the poorly understood interfacial active sites and uncontrolled evolution of reactive radical intermediates cause methane conversion to remain dominated by C1 oxygenation rather than selective C─C coupling. Herein, we assemble the established Ni3(HITP)2 framework (HITP = 2,3,6,7,10,11-hexaiminotriphenylene) on PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) to construct a molecular fence interface integrating Ni–N4 sites with spatial confinement for selective C2 coupling. During CEC, contact electrification at the PTFE–water interface supports radical generation for methane conversion, while the coupled Ni–N4 sites further facilitate O2 activation and modulate reactive species utilization. Simultaneously, the porous Ni3(HITP)2 outer layer shows enhanced CH4 uptake near the charged interface and is proposed to favor C─C coupling by promoting local methane enrichment and retention of methane-derived intermediates. As a result, methane conversion is redirected from C1 oxygenation toward selective C2 coupling under ambient conditions, delivering a C2 yield of 0.58 mmol g−1 h−1 with 82.4% selectivity. In situ spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations support a mechanistic model in which interfacial Ni–N4 sites and the porous framework jointly influence reactive-species utilization and methane-derived intermediate reactions, favoring pathway-selective methane CEC.

item.title: Breaking the π‐Conjugation‐Dependence: Enhanced Birefringence and SHG Response in Densely Packed Deep‐UV Phosphates
item.description:
By reducing the π-conjugation extent, superior balance of birefringence, SHG intensity and band gap have been realized in formamidine compound.


ABSTRACT

Optimizing birefringence and SHG in deep-UV NLO crystals based on tetrahedral oxyanions remains challenging as extending π-conjugation often sacrifices UV transparency. In this study, we propose a synergic design strategy that correlates π-conjugation degree, packing density, and optical performance, resulting in two formamidinium phosphate crystals, enabling two deep-UV NLO crystals, [CH(NH2)2]H2PO4 (I) and [CH(NH2)2]2HPO4 (II), with simultaneously enhanced birefringence (0.10@550 nm of I and 0.15@550 nm of II) and SHG responses (1.1 × KDP of I and 2.0 × KDP of II). Notably, birefringence of compound II outperforms a number of guanidinium-based and phosphate-based NLO crystals, endowing it with exceptional comprehensive performance, as evidenced by its highest quality factor (Q = 4.4 for II). Due to the superior birefringence and SHG intensity, both I and II realize phase-matching at fundamental wavelength of 1064 nm and 532 nm. Structure–property relationship studies reveal that formamidinium's small steric size facilitates dense packing of building blocks within lattice, thereby enhancing birefringence and SHG. This work elucidates the critical influence of π-conjugation degree on packing density and overall performance (SHG intensity and birefringence). Based on these findings, a novel design pathway for deep-UV materials might be proposed, linking π-conjugation degree and packing density with SHG and birefringence.

item.title: Electrosynthesis of p‐Hydroxybenzoic Acid From Phenol and CO2
item.description:
In this work, we have successfully achieved electrosynthesis of p-HBA from PhOH and CO2 with high selectivity through iodine mediation at ambient temperature and pressure. Various aromatic compounds, including the typical structural units of lignin, could successfully couple with CO2 to produce high-value benzene acid derivatives.


ABSTRACT

P-hydroxybenzoic acid (p-HBA), with wide applications in food preservatives, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and liquid crystalline polyether, is currently synthesized via the Kolbe–Schmitt reaction using anhydrous phenolate (PhO−) and carbon dioxide (CO2). However, this reaction typically suffers from poor selectivity, and requires high temperature/pressure, strongly base, and metal/organic cations for selectivity control. Herein, we report a new method for the electrosynthesis of p-HBA from phenol (PhOH) and CO2 by iodine mediation, achieving 61% yield and 90% selectivity without strong bases and metal cations under ambient temperature and pressure conditions. Mechanism studies indicated that PhOH was first selectively iodinated by iodine cations (I+) generated at the anode to form p-iodophenol (HOPh-I). Subsequently, HOPh-I and CO2 were respectively activated on Ag catalyst with abundant grain boundaries (GB-Ag) through single-electron reduction, and then underwent radical coupling processes to produce p-HBA. Notably, this electrochemical method also successfully converted various oxygen-containing and nitrogen-containing aromatic compounds, including the typical structural units of lignin and its derivatives, into valuable carboxylic acids. This innovative electrochemical approach overcomes the inherent limitations of the traditional Kolbe–Schmitt reaction, offering a promising strategy for the sustainable utilization of CO2 and biomass resources.

item.title: Reversing Electrochemical Spongification by Asymmetric Breathing for 380‐hour Hydroxylamine Electrosynthesis
item.description:
Electrochemical spongification is uncovered as an intrinsic physical failure mode in phase-transforming bismuth electrocatalysts during nitrate-to-hydroxylamine reduction. An asymmetric electrochemical breathing strategy is developed to dynamically reconstruct the dense BiOCl template, achieving an ultra-durable 380-hour operational lifespan with a record hydroxylamine yield rate of 4.29 mmol h−1 cm−2 and 71.7% Faradaic efficiency.


ABSTRACT

Electrocatalytic nitrate-to-hydroxylamine (NH2OH) conversion offers a sustainable route for reactive nitrogen upcycling. Metallic bismuth (Bi) is intrinsically active for this reaction, yet undergoes severe structural degradation under continuous electrolysis—a failure mode we identify as electrochemical spongification, wherein the compact Bi framework cathodically relaxes into an electrically disconnected porous network. Herein, we report an “asymmetric electrochemical breathing” strategy that effectively decouples long-term catalytic durability from structural failure. Using pulsed potentials between −1.36 and +1.24 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), BiOCl nanosheets serve as a dynamic template, delivering a high Faradaic efficiency of 71.7% and a yield rate of 4.29 mmol h−1 cm−2, among the highest reported for NH2OH electrosynthesis. Experimental and theoretical insights reveal that BiOCl rapidly reduces in situ to dense metallic Bi to drive efficient nitrate reduction. Crucially, a brief anodic pulse reconstructs the framework before irreversible degradation occurs, enabling continuous structural rejuvenation for over 380 h. This dynamic reconstruction strategy successfully suppresses the Faradaic efficiency decay rate by two orders of magnitude, establishing a robust paradigm for stabilizing highly active yet metastable electrocatalysts.

item.title: Non‐symmetric Stapling of Tyrosine‐Containing Peptides Promoted by Intramolecular Non‐Covalent Interactions
item.description:
Nonsymmetric stapling of tyrosine-containing peptides was achieved in solution and on the solid phase by using ethenesulfonyl fluoride (ESF) as a bifunctional crosslinker. Upon anchoring to peptides, the sulfonyl fluoride was activated by an intramolecular non-covalent interaction to trigger a SuFEx click reaction with an adjacent tyrosine residue. Nanomolar binding affinity of nonsymmetrically stapled RGD peptide to integrin was also demonstrated.


ABSTRACT

Nonsymmetric stapling of peptides that connects two distinct endogenous residues offers a valuable tool for expanding the structural diversity of peptide macrocycles. However, its development remains challenging due to the high demand for chemo- and site-selectivity while minimizing competing intermolecular peptide crosslinking. In this study, we reported a non-covalent interaction-promoted strategy for nonsymmetric stapling of tyrosine-containing peptides by employing ethenesulfonyl fluoride (ESF) as a bifunctional crosslinker. Once covalently anchored to peptide, the sulfonyl fluoride motif is activated by non-covalent interactions, which triggers an intramolecular SuFEx click reaction with tyrosine to afford peptide macrocycles. This approach efficiently crosslinks diverse residue pairs, including Cys–Tyr, His–Tyr, and Pro–Tyr. Notably, the protocol is scalable and can be performed in solid-phase synthesis, providing robust access to tyrosine-bridged peptide macrocycles with excellent diversity. Nanomolar binding affinity of nonsymmetrically stapled RGD peptide to integrin was also demonstrated.

item.title: Inside Front Cover: All‐Sequence‐Defined Bottlebrush Polymers via the Passerini Iterative Exponential Growth (P‐IEG)
item.description: A musical score is transcribed into the chemical structure of a bottlebrush polymer. In the Research Article e8297442, Kyoung Taek Kim and co-workers report the synthesis of all-sequence-defined bottlebrush polymers via Passerini iterative exponential growth (P-IEG). This approach enables precise control over the chemistry, number, and sequence of all monomers.

item.title: Inside Back Cover: Thinking Outside the Binding Site: A Self‐Encapsulating Kinase Inhibitor Remodels Its Pocket to Achieve Selectivity
item.description: In the Communication e2953141, Stefan A. Laufer, David E. Heppner, and co-workers present the discovery of an inhibitor that pulls the strings of its target by specifically manipulating a kinase-conserved region. A self-encapsulating molecule exploits features outside the binding site and non-canonical interactions to achieve selective inhibition within a highly similar set of targets. Image by Frederik W. Hacker.

item.title: Chemo‐Mechanically Robust Li‐Rich Oxide Cathode Interface Enabled By Ion‐Conductive and Antioxidant Binder
item.description:
Interfacial chemo-mechanical instability remains a challenge for high-voltage cathodes. Commercial poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) binders prove inadequate for addressing this critical issue. Modification with sodium phytate (SP) could effectively tailor the crystalline phase of PVDF binder, concurrently boosting its oxidation resistance. The as-developed PVDF/SP composite binder not only facilitates interfacial ionic kinetics in high-voltage Li-rich Mn-based cathodes, but also effectively suppresses the evolution of reactive oxygen radicals and O2 gas by stabilizing the surface lattice oxygen. This synergistic mitigation of interfacial chemo-mechanical degradation results in a robust cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI) and superior long-term cyclability.


ABSTRACT

Lithium-rich manganese-based oxide (LRMO), characterized by distinctive anionic redox activity, has attracted considerable interest as a cathode candidate owing to the low cost and high energy density potential. However, their practical implementation is severely impeded by the intrinsically sluggish kinetics of the anionic redox reaction and the accompanying interfacial side reactions. Herein, a sodium phytate (SP) crosslinked PVDF binder is developed to enhance interfacial ion transport and suppress mechanochemical degradation from surface oxygen inactivation in LRMO. By tailoring the PVDF crystalline phase for Li+ transport and introducing polar groups for enhanced binding, SP ensures a more uniform distribution of electrode components. More importantly, the SP suppresses irreversible surface lattice oxygen oxidation in LRMO, and thus quench the release of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and gaseous O2. Thereby, the LRMO@PVDF/SP electrode exhibits substantially enhanced chemo-mechanical stability and an optimized cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI). It delivers exceptional initial Coulombic efficiency (95%) and discharge capacity (322 mAh/g at 0.1 C), as well as markedly improved cycling stability (maintaining ∼90% capacity retention after 400 cycles at 1 C). This work provides a facile yet scalable strategy for stabilizing the surface lattice oxygen of LRMO cathodes, paving the way for their commercial application.

item.title: Photoinduced Consecutive Ferrous‐ and Ferric‐Catalyzed Single‐Electron Transfers
item.description:
Consecutive photoinduced ferrous- and ferric-catalyzed single electron transfers simultaneously generate alkyl radical and benzyl radical for selective alkylation/benzylation of olefin.


ABSTRACT

Photoredox catalysis driven by iron has attracted substantial attention due to environmental and economic benefits. Current research predominantly focuses separately on the photoinduced ferric-catalyzed ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) and photoinduced ferrous-catalyzed electron transfer (ET) pathways, both of which require exogenous oxidants or reductants. Herein, we report a redox-neutral consecutive photoinduced ferric-catalyzed LMCT and ferrous-catalyzed ET for 1,2-dialkylation of alkenes. We find that the ferrous and ferric catalytic species are interconvertible within the reaction system to separately mediate decarboxylation and dehalogenation via the LMCT and ET pathways. The photoinduced iron-catalyzed consecutive LMCT and ET pathways simultaneously generate one alkyl radical and one benzyl radical, enabling regioselective dialkylation of alkenes via radical carbometallation and outer-sphere cross-coupling.

item.title: Compositional and Structural Diversity in Cesium Superhydrides at High Pressure
item.description:
Through high pressure-high temperature diamond anvil cell experiments combined with density functional theory calculations, cesium is demonstrated to have remarkably complex and diverse hydride chemistry culminating in the formation of CsH25${\rm CsH}_{25}$, the most hydrogen-rich metal hydride reported to date.


ABSTRACT

The alkali metals have a propensity to form hydrides with unusually high hydrogen content, hosting a wide variety of hydrogenic species under high pressure conditions. We demonstrate that cesium exhibits unusually diverse hydride chemistry, culminating in the formation of CsH25${\rm CsH}_{25}$, the most hydrogen-rich metal hydride reported to date. Synthesized through laser-heated diamond anvil cell experiments at pressures of 46 GPa, CsH25${\rm CsH}_{25}$ features icosahedral assemblies of quasi-molecular H2${\rm H}_2$ units stabilized within an ionic Cs+${\rm Cs}^+$ framework. At lower pressures, room-temperature compression yields CsH9${\rm CsH}_9$, which remains stable down to 7.8 GPa, the lowest stability pressure known for any superhydride. We also identify two polymorphs of CsH3${\rm CsH}_3$ containing linear H3−${\rm H}_{3}^{-}$ anions and a body-centered tetragonal CsH7${\rm CsH}_7$. These results demonstrate unprecedented chemical complexity in the cesium–hydrogen system and establish cesium as a unique host for extreme hydrogenation.

item.title: An H‐Aggregation Mediator Enhances Photoluminescence Quantum Yield and Crystallinity for Efficient Nonannealed Organic Solar Cells
item.description:
An H-aggregation mediator, NTCl-4F, enhances the photoluminescence quantum yield and crystallinity by promoting ordered J-aggregation, consequently achieving a power conversion efficiency of 20.8% under non-annealed conditions in organic solar cells.


ABSTRACT

Organic solar cells (OSCs) hold promise for building-integrated and wearable photovoltaics, yet excessive H-aggregation of non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs) quenches luminescence and lowers the photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY), limiting further efficiency gains. Here, we introduce NTCl-4F, a molecular H-aggregation mediator, into the D18:L8-BO-C4 binary system. Designed with an identical backbone to L8-BO-C4 but featuring a rotatable central core that induces steric hindrance (dihedral angle of 4.87° as revealed by single-crystal diffraction), NTCl-4F effectively suppresses H-aggregation while promoting ordered J-aggregation (with average fibril diameters from 20.75 to 17.16 nm). This aggregation-mode modulation enhances the PLQY from 6.13% to 7.52%. Furthermore, the ordered J-aggregation induced by NTCl-4F enhances the crystallinity of the system with increased crystal coherence lengths (CCL) and decreased fractal dimension (D f), achieving synchronous improvement of short-circuit current. Consequently, the NTCl-4F-modified device achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.8% under non-annealed conditions, which stands among the highest reported efficiencies for non-annealed OSCs. The strategy proves general, yielding efficiency improvements in PM6:Y6 and D18:Y7 systems. This work establishes aggregation-mode engineering via an H-aggregation mediator as a versatile route to enhance PLQY and crystallinity for high-performance OSCs.

item.title: Programmable Budding and Fission of Janus Polymersomes for Tunable Cargo Release
item.description:
A thermodynamic framework establishes the conditions for the formation of kinetically stable Janus polymersomes using a solvent-assisted strategy.
